claims.text: Adding SiC particulate to a ZrB2 matrix and spark-plasma sintering below 1700 °C will reduce the required densification temperature.
The SiC-containing composite will have better oxidation resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
The SiC-containing composite will have better liquid-metal corrosion resistance than single-phase ZrB2 and prior lower-temperature specimens.
High-purity commercial ZrB2 powder with submicron-to-micron particles is an applicable starting material.
The intervention uses approximately 10–20 vol% fine SiC particles in ZrB2.
The composite is to be consolidated by spark plasma sintering at approximately 1600–1700 °C under an inert atmosphere.
A pressure of at least 40 MPa and a sufficient hold time will produce near-full density.
The resulting material is applicable in oxidizing atmospheres up to approximately 1500 °C.
SiC partially reacts with ZrB2 to form stable interfacial phases.
SiC contributes to formation of a protective scale during oxidation and corrosion.
The SiC-derived interfacial structure enhances grain-boundary strength and inhibits rapid diffusion paths.
Stable multicomponent phases and a continuous surface scale containing Si-based oxides and higher-order borides will form.
The proposed surface scale will limit oxidation and liquid-metal infiltration.
The composite will densify at a temperature 200–400 °C lower than the relevant comparison materials.
The composite will achieve flexural strength greater than 500 MPa.
Pure ZrB2 typically requires at least 2300 °C to achieve sufficient density.
ZrB2 processed at approximately 1700 °C has limited oxidation and corrosion resistance.
The composite will remain stable in liquid plating metals at moderate temperatures.
SiC contents above 20 vol% may introduce free carbon or brittle phases.
The cited evidence does not directly establish improved liquid-metal corrosion resistance from SiC addition to ZrB2.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis specifies sub-1700 °C consolidation, but the intervention and experiment permit a temperature of 1700 °C.

Reducing the stated baseline of at least 2300 °C to 1600–1700 °C corresponds to a reduction of at least 600–700 °C, not the claimed 200–400 °C; the alternative comparison underlying the smaller reduction is not specified.
